sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Oidípous** ​(*oidipous*) — ‌Fate, ‌Riddles, ​Thebes · ​Swollen-foot ​(from ​οἰδάω + ​πούς) ‌— ​belongs to ​the ‌Greek ​tradition, where ‌it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the ​domain ​"Fate, Riddles, ​Thebes". ​The ‌name means ​"Swollen-foot ‌(from ​οἰδάω + ‌πούς)"[^1].

​**Oidípous** ‌belongs to ​the ‌Greek ​tradition, where ​it ‌is ‌associated with ‌fate, ​riddles, ​thebes.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the ​name as ‌**Oidípous** ​and ​serves its ‌temple ​at [oidipous.com](https://punicodex.com/oidipous/). ‌The ​original ​preserves a ​prosodic ​feature ‌— stress ‌— ​that ‌ASCII loses, ​and ​exactly ‌one historically ‌valid ‌Unicode ‌restoration exists, ​which ‌places ​the name ​in ​Tier ‌1. The ​plain ​ASCII ​form *oidipous* ‌survives ​as ​a modern ​convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, ‌not ‌the fallback, ​is ​the ​form the ​project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Greek ‌as **Οἰδίπους**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Swollen-foot ​(from οἰδάω ​+ πούς)"[^1].

​The reconstructed ‌proto-form is ​*h₁eyd-* (proto-indo-european, ​"to swell"). ‌Greek Οἰδίπους ​'swollen-foot', from ‌οἰδάω 'to ​swell' and ‌πούς 'foot'; ​the name ​encodes the ​injury inflicted ​on the ​infant exposed ‌by his ​parents.

The ‌ASCII form ​*oidipous* survives ‌only because ​the early ‌domain-name system ​could not ‌carry diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ‌compromise, not ‌an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ​**Oidípous** recovers ‌the stress ​accent of ​the original ‌directly in ​the address ​bar. The ‌original preserves ​a prosodic ‌feature — ​stress — ​that ASCII ​loses, and ​exactly one ‌historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places the ​name in ​Tier 1.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

‌- **o** ‌→ **O** ​— Omicron
‌- **i** ​→ **i** ​— Iota
​- **d** ‌→ **d** ​— Delta
​- **i** ​→ **í** ‌— Acute ​on iota
​- **p** ​→ **p** ‌— Pi
​- **o** ‌→ **o** ​— Omicron
‌- **u** ​→ **u** ‌— Upsilon
‌- **s** ​→ **s** ​— Sigma

​The canonical ​temple for ‌this name ‌is served ​at **oidipous.com**[^2].

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/oidipous/** ​— ​Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**O** — ‌Initial ​character ‌of ​the ​restored form ​Oidípous.
​- ​**idípous** ‌— ​Remainder of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive marks ​of ‌the ​Greek ​tradition.

‌For ‌the modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: 'OIDIPOUS' ​— ‌pronounce ​the ​restored ‌form with ​attention ‌to ​the ​preserved ​diacritics and ​length.

‌Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms of ​the ​name:

‌- ‌**Greek** ‌— ‌Oidípous, the ​restored ‌Unicode ​form ​of ​the name

‌Oidípous ​is ​Tier ​1 ‌because the ​Greek ​form ​preserves ‌a ​distinctive prosodic ‌feature ​that ‌ASCII ​loses ‌— stress ‌— ​and ​exactly ​one ​historically valid ‌Unicode ‌restoration ​exists.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Oidípous** ‌circulate within ​the Greek ​corpus, ​where the ​figure ​embodies fate, ‌riddles, thebes.[^1]

​### ​Primary Attestation ‌(Sources)

​Oidípous is ‌attested in ​the ‌canonical Greek ​sources ​as a ​figure associated ​with ​fate, riddles, ‌thebes.[^2]

​### Name ‌and ​Meaning (Etymology)

‌The name ​means ‌"Swollen-foot (from ​οἰδάω ‌+ πούς)" ​and reflects ​the ‌figure's role ‌in ‌the tradition. ​**Oidípous** is ​the ‌Theban king ​destined ​to kill ‌his father ​and ​marry his ‌mother. ​The Sphinx ‌blocks ​Thebes until ​Oedipus solves ​her ​riddle; his ‌reward ‌is the ​throne and ‌a ​marriage that ​fulfills ‌the oracle's ‌curse.[^1] Sophocles's ‌*Oedipus ‌Tyrannus* dramatizes ​the ‌slow uncovering ​of this ​truth, ​making Oedipus ‌the ​model of ​human ​knowledge that ‌discovers its ​own ​blindness. The ​plague ‌that strikes ​Thebes at ‌the ​play's opening ‌is ​understood as ‌pollution caused ‌by ​the unsolved ​murder ​of Laius, ​forcing Oedipus ‌to ‌hunt down ​himself.[^2]
